LEAGUE INVESTIGATES COACH WHO ALLEGEDLY CHARGED PARENTS FOR GUARANTEED PLAYING TIME

CINCINNATI, OH — Youth league coach Bill Osterhoudt, 47, is under investigation after several parents reported he had been privately charging a fee in exchange for guaranteeing their children a set amount of playing time each game, undermining the league's standard rotation policy.

League officials say the arrangement came to light after a parent who declined to pay noticed their child's playing time dropped noticeably compared to kids whose families had quietly paid.

Charged fifty dollars per season for a guaranteed minimum playing time
Collected payments in cash directly before each game began
Adjusted the standard rotation to favor paying families consistently
Denied any wrongdoing, calling it "a fair way to reward commitment"
Continued the practice for two full seasons before parents compared notes
Offered a "playoff guarantee" upgrade for an additional twenty dollars
Kept a private spreadsheet tracking which families had paid each season

Parents who paid reportedly assumed the fee was some kind of official league requirement until non-paying families started asking questions.

League commissioner Renata Falkowski, thirteen years overseeing youth sports, said, "I've mediated disputes over playing time before. I've never had a coach turn it into a paid subscription service."

The rotation chart, now under review, declined to comment.

The league says playing time will be strictly standardized going forward, payment or no payment.

text:
Waymo will begin testing robotaxis in Greater Cincinnati (paving the way for Tesla)

Story from the Cincinnati Business Courier...

"Waymo, the company that has launched its driverless robotaxis in 14 metropolitan markets, will "soon" begin testing its vehicles in Cincinnati with an eye toward launching local service sometime in the future.

Waymo’s trained “autonomous specialists” will manually drive Jaguar I-PACE vehicles around downtown, Northern Kentucky and surrounding areas. The purpose is to create a high-definition map of the area, a first step to running Waymo’s technology in a new city.

“Waymo is here in Cincinnati to begin mapping the city and the surrounding area,” Waymo spokesman Chris Bonelli said.

Waymo will map the area and then leave when that project is complete, Bonelli added.

“When we are ready to return, we’ll reach out and share more,” he said.

Waymo typically starts with human drivers behind the wheel, mapping a region’s roads for the company’s navigation system. Then Waymo employees ride in the vehicles while the cars drive themselves in a second test phase. Once that is complete, the service is open to the public.

Waymo’s service is similar to Uber and Lyft where riders call for a car via a mobile app.

The company offered its first autonomous ride in Austin, Texas, in 2015. Waymo currently is active in San Francisco; Los Angeles; Phoenix; Austin; Atlanta; Dallas; Houston; San Antonio; Miami; Orlando, Fla.; Nashville, Tenn.; Denver, San Diego; and Tampa, Fla.

It surpassed 20 million fully autonomous trips companywide in December 2025 and has notched over 200 million driverless miles, according to the company.

In February, Waymo raised more than $16 billion in funding, the large majority of it from Alphabet Inc., according to U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission filings reported by the Business Courier’s sister news organization, the Denver Business Journal.

The company frequently cites peer-reviewed research it conducted that found its vehicles had 94% fewer serious-injury crashes compared to human drivers."

text:
The State presented a number of witnesses concerning what they described as Leo Frank’s lewd, lecherous, licentious, and lascivious conduct toward women and girls. Thomas E. Watson later repeated many of these accusations in his August 1915 Watson’s Magazine article. Much of what Watson wrote can be traced to sworn testimony reported in the Atlanta newspapers in 1913. Some of his stronger claims need more caution because the newspapers either give a narrower account or do not print the allegation at all.

WHERE THE EVENTS WERE SAID TO HAVE HAPPENED

The Atlanta Journal of Friday, August 8, 1913, in “Defense Attacks State’s Case From Many Angles,” page 1, column 1, published a model of the National Pencil Company building. Leo Frank’s private office was on the second floor. The women’s dressing room was on the fourth floor. The basement contained the boiler, partition, elevator shaft, ladder, and other areas later discussed by witnesses (AJ, 10).

NELLIE PETTIS

Nellie Pettis testified under oath at the coroner’s inquest on Friday, May 9, 1913.

The Atlanta Georgian, in “Best Detective in America Now is on Case, Says Dorsey,” page 2, reported that Pettis went to the factory to collect her sister-in-law’s wages. She said Leo Frank pulled out a box containing money, looked at the money, looked at her, winked, and asked, “How about it?” Pettis said she understood this as an improper proposition and left his office (AG, 2).

The incident took place in Leo Frank’s office on the second floor.

Watson later repeated the same basic story, saying Pettis testified that Leo Frank showed her money, winked, and propositioned her. On this point Watson’s account closely follows testimony already printed in the Atlanta Georgian more than two years earlier (WM, 11; AG, 2).

NELLIE WOOD

Nellie Wood testified at the same coroner’s inquest.

The Atlanta Georgian reported that Wood had worked at the National Pencil Company for only two days. She said Leo Frank called her into his second-floor office, tried to close the door, moved close to her, and touched her. Asked where, Wood answered, “He barely touched my breast.” She said she resisted his advances and soon left the factory (AG, 2).

Watson later printed a longer version involving alleged attempts to touch her breast, lower limbs (euphemism for private parts), and dress (euphemism below the belt). The May 9 newspaper independently confirms the office encounter, physical touching, and Wood’s resistance, but it does not print every detail Watson later gave (WM, 11; AG, 2).

THE FOURTH-FLOOR DRESSING ROOM

Irene Jackson, a defense witness, testified about Leo Frank entering the women’s dressing room on the fourth floor during the designated changing time.

The Atlanta Journal of Saturday, August 16, 1913, in “Witness, Called by Defense, Testifies Against Frank,” reported that Jackson said Leo Frank opened the dressing-room door without knocking while girls were changing clothes. She described one occasion when Emily Mayfield had removed her outer dress. Jackson also agreed that one incident happened during the girls’ regular changing time (AJ, 3).

Mamie Kitchens later supported the central part of Jackson’s account. The Atlanta Journal of Wednesday, August 20, 1913, in “Testimony May Close Wednesday: Both Sides Are Anxious To Begin Argument And Send Case To The Jury,” beginning page 1, column 6, reported that Kitchens was in the fourth-floor dressing room with Irene Jackson when Leo Frank opened the door without knocking. Kitchens said Jackson was undressed, Leo Frank grinned, and Jackson protested, “We’re dressing, blame it!” (AJ, 4).

The defense brought out that Leo Frank also asked whether the girls had work to do. Kitchens said it was during working hours, but the girls had no work at that moment.

REBECCA CARSON, MYRTICE CATO, AND MAGGIE GRIFFIN

Rebecca Carson denied ever entering the fourth-floor dressing room with Leo Frank.

The State called Myrtice Cato and Maggie Griffin to contradict her.

The Atlanta Constitution of Thursday, August 21, 1913, in “Girls Testify to Seeing Frank Enter Dressing Room With Woman,” page 2, reported that the jury was first excused while the lawyers argued before Judge Leonard S. Roan over whether the testimony could be admitted (AC, 5).

Cato testified that she had seen Carson and Leo Frank enter the dressing room together twice. One incident was about 10 o’clock in the morning and another occurred in the afternoon. Asked how she saw them, Cato answered, “I looked up the aisle” (AJ, 4; AC, 5).

Griffin testified that she had seen Carson and Leo Frank enter the fourth-floor dressing room together three or four times during working hours (AJ, 4; AC, 5).

Griffin also gave an estimate of fifteen to thirty minutes for how long they remained inside, but Judge Roan ruled that answer out. It should therefore not be presented as evidence left before the jury (AJ, 4).

Watson was correct that Cato and Griffin testified about Carson entering the dressing room with Leo Frank. Watson was incorrect when he said the defense did not question them. Rosser cross-examined both women (WM, 11; AJ, 4; AC, 5).

THE STATE’S CHARACTER WITNESSES

The Atlanta Constitution of Thursday, August 21, 1913, in “Frank’s Character Bad Declare Many Women and Girls on Stand,” page 2, reported that the State called a number of women to attack Leo Frank’s general character and his character for lasciviousness (AC, 1).

Among them were Myrtice Cato, Maggie Griffin, Marie Karst, Nellie Pettis, Mary Davis, Mary E. Wallace, Estelle Winkle, Carrie Smith, Ruth Robinson, Dewey Hewell, and others.

The Constitution reported that Nellie Pettis, Mary Davis, Mary E. Wallace, and Estelle Winkle testified that Leo Frank’s character for lasciviousness was bad (AC, 1).

C. B. DALTON, THE OFFICE, AND THE BASEMENT

C. B. Dalton testified for the State on Thursday, August 7, 1913.

The Atlanta Journal, in “Dr. Harris Testimony is Attacked by Defense Expert,” reported that Dalton said he had visited the National Pencil Company “four or five times with Daisy Hopkins” (AJ, 9).

Dalton said he entered the office area and saw Leo Frank there. He then went with Hopkins into the basement. Using the factory diagram, Dalton pointed to an enclosure behind the partition beside the boiler. He said he reached the basement by the ladder near the elevator rather than the rear stairs (AJ, 9).

Dalton also testified that he had seen women in Leo Frank’s office, sometimes two or more, and said beer was present on one occasion. He said he gave Jim Conley a quarter during his visits (AJ, 9).

Dalton did not testify that he knew Leo Frank was aware of what happened in the basement. He specifically said he did not know whether Leo Frank knew he was there.

JIM CONLEY’S LOOKOUT STORY

The stronger claim that Leo Frank arranged these visits came from Jim Conley.

The Atlanta Journal of Monday, August 4, 1913, in “Jim Conley Tells An Amazing Story,” beginning page 1, column 1, reported Conley’s claim that Leo Frank once offered him money to watch the front door while a woman and Dalton entered the factory (AJ, 8).

Conley said the pair later went through the building and descended by ladder into the basement. He claimed Leo Frank had instructed him to open the way for them.

Conley also described another Saturday when Daisy Hopkins entered the building and went to Leo Frank’s office. Conley said Leo Frank signaled him to watch the front door and later paid him (AJ, 8).

This is the newspaper testimony that most closely supports Watson’s claim that Conley acted as a lookout while women visited the factory.

DAISY HOPKINS DENIED IT

Daisy Hopkins denied the Dalton-Conley story.

The Atlanta Journal of Friday, August 8, 1913, “Defense Attacks State’s Case From Many Angles,” page 1, column 7, continuing on page 4, column 1, reported that Hopkins denied ever going into Leo Frank’s office for drinks, visiting the factory with Dalton, introducing Dalton to Leo Frank, or going into the basement with him (AJ, 10).

Any account of Dalton and Conley should include her denial.

DEWEY HEWELL BROUGHT FROM CINCINNATI, OHIO

The Atlanta Journal of Friday, August 15, 1913, “Leo M. Frank Ready to Tell His Own Story to Jury,” page 1, column 1, carried the subheadline:

“ATLANTA GIRL BROUGHT FROM REFORMATORY IN CINCINNATI TO TESTIFY AGAINST FRANK.”

The Journal identified the girl as sixteen-year-old Dewey Hewell and said police matron Bohnefeld had brought her from the Home of the Good Shepherd in Cincinnati, Ohio, to testify for the State (AJ, 7).

The newspaper said the exact nature of her expected testimony had not been learned.

WHAT HEWELL TOLD THE JURY

The Atlanta Constitution of Thursday, August 21, 1913, in “Girls Testify to Seeing Leo Frank Talking to Little Mary Phagan With His Hands on Her Person,” page 2, reported Hewell’s testimony (AC, 6).

Hewell said she had worked at the National Pencil Company and knew Mary Phagan and Leo Frank. She testified that she had seen Leo Frank talking to Mary several times in a day. She said he called Mary by her first name, stood close to her, leaned toward her face, and placed his hand on her shoulder (AC, 6).

The Atlanta Journal’s August 20 report gives substantially the same account and places these observations in the metal department (AJ, 4).

Rosser brought out on cross-examination that other girls were present and that Hewell did not know what Leo Frank and Mary were discussing.

WATSON’S INNER-THIGH CLAIM

Watson’s August 1915 account went much further.

Watson wrote that Hewell had claimed Leo Frank “ruined her” and that, while the jury was absent, Judge Roan heard testimony about “a scar on her inner thigh made by his teeth” (WM, 11).

Several surrounding parts of Watson’s story are independently supported by the newspapers.

Hewell had worked at the National Pencil Company. She was sixteen years old. She was living at the Home of the Good Shepherd in Cincinnati, Ohio. Police matron Bohnefeld traveled there and brought her back to Atlanta specifically to testify for the State. She appeared during the State’s rebuttal. The newspapers also show that Judge Roan sometimes excused the jury while lawyers argued over evidence concerning specific alleged sexual conduct (AJ, 7; AC, 5; AC, 6).

What I have not found in the Atlanta Constitution, Atlanta Journal, or Atlanta Georgian from August 1913 is an article printing Watson’s exact claim about a bite scar on Hewell’s inner thigh. Though family verbal history supports this claim as being true.

That written detail should therefore remain attributed directly to Watson.

CONCLUSION

Watson’s August 1915 account rests partly on testimony that can be checked directly against the 1913 newspapers.

The Pettis accusation is well supported by the Atlanta Georgian.

The basic Nellie Wood account is also supported, although Watson gives more detail than the newspaper.

The Cato and Griffin testimony about Rebecca Carson entering the fourth-floor dressing room with Leo Frank is confirmed by the Atlanta Constitution and Atlanta Journal. Watson was wrong, however, in saying the defense did not question them.

Dalton testified about visiting the factory with Daisy Hopkins, seeing women in Leo Frank’s office, and going into the basement. Conley supplied the stronger allegation that Leo Frank used him as a lookout. Hopkins denied both men’s story.

Hewell’s public testimony about Leo Frank’s familiarity with Mary Phagan is clearly reported. Her trip from the Home of the Good Shepherd in Cincinnati, Ohio, is also well documented.

Watson’s exact claim about a scar on Hewell’s inner thigh caused by Leo Frank’s teeth remains different. The newspapers support much of the setting around the story, but I have not found a 1913 Atlanta newspaper that independently prints that specific allegation.

text:
In a previous post,  the Ed Iskenderian's story was mentioned. The Camfather. Born 1921. Died 2026 at 104. Founded Isky Racing Cams from a single cam grinding machine in 1946. First president of SEMA. "From one hot rodder to another." What was mentioned in one sentence but never expanded is where Iskenderian learned the trade. He learned it from Ed Winfield. The man who showed the Camfather how to build a grinding machine was the man who had invented the American performance camshaft three decades before the Camfather ever touched one. Winfield is the root of the tree. Iskenderian is the trunk. Every camshaft company that followed is a branch. And the root was planted in 1919 by a man from Jennings, Louisiana, who built his first gasoline engine at age sixteen.
Ed Winfield was born April 16, 1885, moved to Los Angeles in 1910, and entered a city that was about to become the center of American automotive speed culture. The dry lake beds surrounding LA, Muroc and El Mirage and the Rosamond flats were already attracting speed seekers running modified cars on the hard packed desert surface. Winfield recognized that the camshaft was the most important component in determining an engine's character and output, and in 1919 he introduced his legendary "Maximotor" camshaft, a profile designed to increase valve lift and duration beyond factory specifications for improved breathing and higher RPM potential. The Maximotor became the first widely recognized aftermarket performance camshaft in America. Before Isky. Before Howard. Before Comp Cams. Before Crane. Before every cam company that exists today. Winfield ground the first one.
Then he did the same thing with carburetors. Recognizing that a better cam without a better fuel delivery system only solved half the airflow equation, Winfield designed and manufactured the Winfield carburetor, a precision downdraft unit with a variable venturi that allowed racers to adjust the air-fuel mixture for different conditions without changing jets. The variable venturi was decades ahead of its time, offering a level of tunability that factory carburetors couldn't match. The combination of Winfield cam and Winfield carburetor became the standard setup for serious racers on the West Coast through the 1920s and 1930s. Winfield controlled both sides of the intake equation: the cam determined when the valves opened and the carburetor determined what flowed through them. Nobody else offered both.
The racing resume validated the components. Winfield's camshafts powered Frank Lockhart's Stutz Black Hawk Special at Indianapolis in the late 1920s. His components were omnipresent in midget racing, sprint car racing, dry lakes competition, and the emerging hot rod culture of Southern California. During World War II, Winfield applied his understanding of combustion and airflow to aircraft engine development, the same wartime crossover that created the Corvair's aviation future and the Ford GAA tank engine's civilian afterlife. After the war, Winfield's shop became the gathering point for the next generation of speed equipment manufacturers, including the young Ed Iskenderian who came looking for a camshaft and left with the knowledge to build his own.
The Winfield-to-Iskenderian handoff is the most important mentorship in American performance history. Winfield told Iskenderian he could see from his questions that the young man was going to be big in the camshaft business. Then Winfield showed him how to build a cam grinding machine. The mentor armed the student who would eventually build a larger company, a louder brand, and a more famous name. But the knowledge came from Winfield. The cam profiles that Iskenderian refined and marketed were built on the principles that Winfield had established in 1919. The Camfather inherited the science from the man who invented it.
Winfield was inducted posthumously into the Motorsports Hall of Fame of America in 2012. He enrolled in engineering courses at USC to formalize the knowledge he had gained through decades of hands-on experimentation. He worked alongside Howard "Howdy" Wilcox, the renowned race car driver. He built components that found their way into engines around the world. And he established the fundamental principle that every engine builder on this page operates by: the camshaft is the engine's personality, and the person who controls the cam profile controls the power. Before there was an Isky cam. Before there was a Comp cam. Before there was a Crane cam. There was a Winfield cam. The original. 1919. Everything after it is a descendant.

text:
The Ark-La-Tex may be leading America’s lithium race | Dugan Flanakin, CFACT

The discovery of vast lithium resources in the Smackover Formation, most notably in southern Arkansas and far into northern Louisiana and across northeast Texas, has sparked widespread interest among corporations and community leaders in all three states.

Last year, the Venture Center, Standard Lithium, and the University of Arkansas launched the Arkansas Lithium Technology Accelerator (ALTA), the nation’s first accelerator program dedicated to lithium and battery supply-chain innovation. Then, in July, the first State of Lithium Symposium was held in Texarkana to examine the future of lithium mining in Texas.

Not to be outdone, Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry, on August 20, signed two executive orders that fast-track environmental permitting for critical minerals and rare-earth production. The first requires state agencies to examine which permits can be permanently expedited. The second declares heavy rare-earth extraction and advanced chemical processing to be vital to local job creation and national defense.

Excitement across the Ark-La-Tex stems from the fact that the heaviest concentrations of lithium in the Smackover Foundation lie in a band from southern Arkansas (crossing into far northwest Louisiana) and far northeast Texas. Arkansas is farthest along, but Texas is itching to join in an economic boom that could also spread into north Louisiana.

The Ark-La-Tex has long been a major U.S. oil and gas hub, but the region has recently suffered a downturn in drilling activity, production growth, and economic impact. This, coupled with the national emphasis on critical minerals, has refocused regional leaders on the hope that lithium extraction will rekindle local economies and bring new prosperity.

Executive Order 13817, which President Trump issued early in 2017, authorized creation of a federal strategy to ensure secure and reliable supplies of critical minerals and break America’s dependence on China for 21st Century technological progress.

Political enemies have fought against the Trump critical minerals agenda from Day 1. Until Trump won a second term, progress toward achieving EO 13817’s goals was stymied.

To reset his reshoring agenda, President Trump in January 2025 issued Executive Order 14154, Unleashing American Energy, which established the U.S. position that it should be the leading producer and processor of non-fuel minerals, including rare-earth minerals.

Two months later, Executive Order 14241 announced immediate measures to increase American minerals production. The EO stated that overbearing federal regulations had crippled the nation’s minerals industries and forced increasing reliance on hostile foreign powers for the minerals critical to the auto, semiconductor, and power industries.

The President upped the ante on August 13, 2025, when the Department of Energy made available nearly $1 billion in funding to advance and scale mining, processing, and manufacturing technologies across key stages of critical minerals and materials supply chains. A few days ago the DOE announced $162 million for nine projects that will recover critical minerals, materials, and other byproducts from industrial feedstocks.

One of these critical minerals is lithium, which is used in high-performance batteries for electric vehicles, grid storage systems, and consumer electronics as well as in the production of metals, ceramics, and pharmaceuticals – and in the aerospace and defense industries. While there are ample lithium resources inside the U.S., in 2025 the nation relied on imports – mainly from Chile and Argentina – for more than half its lithium consumption.

Lithium can be mined from hard rock ore in the form of lithium spodumene or extracted as an ion from briny water. China, which possesses 95% of the world’s hard-rock lithium, has long controlled 70% to 80% of the global electric vehicle lithium-ion battery market. Unless the U.S. dramatically increases its own lithium production, prioritizing electric vehicles benefits an increasingly hostile Chinese government.

Hard-rock lithium production began in North Carolina and became important during World War II for hydrogen production, high-temperature lubrication, and carbon dioxide absorption until outpriced by cheaper, brine-based lithium facilities. Today the Kings Mountain facility is only used for lithium conversion and research. But in 2024, Albermarle Corporation began work to reopen the mine after receiving a $90 million grant from the Department of Defense.

The only active U.S. lithium production operation today is Albemarle Corporation’s Clayton Valley facility in southwestern Nevada. Since 1966, brine extracted from saltwater aquifers has flowed into evaporation ponds, where the lithium is concentrated in multiple solar evaporation ponds for up to 24 months.

The Biden DOE, in October 2024, issued a $2.26 billion loan to Lithium Nevada Corp to expedite lithium carbonate production at a facility adjacent to the Thacker Pass lithium mine in northern Nevada, home to the largest U.S. lithium deposit. Last year, the Trump DOE negotiated a 5% equity ownership in Lithium Americas in exchange for deferring $182 million of debt service.

Even so, all the buzz today over the potential of lithium to lift spirits and fill pocketbooks is in the Ark-La-Tex. It began even before Exxon Mobil in 2023 announced plans to build one of the world’s largest lithium processing facilities near Magnolia, Arkansas, with a capacity to produce 75,000 to 100,000 metric tons a year of lithium carbonate –twice as much as at Thacker Pass.

ALTA has since sponsored three cohorts, each involving multiple companies, to showcase Arkansas’s promotion of lithium production and offer support to companies in sustainable lithium extraction, advanced battery technology, and recycling. Arkansas had folded its lithium production regulations in a network long established for oil- and gas-related brine production.

The July Texas lithium symposium was a first step toward a legislative campaign to set rules for lithium extraction and processing in the Lone Star State. East Texas lithium producers plan to rely on a new technique – direct lithium extraction – that does not involve solar evaporation. This means reinjection of the spent brine, which in Texas today means back from where it came.

Industry representatives, however, say this would dilute lithium concentrations in the brine and force frequent relocation of operations. They are seeking legislative changes in 2027, using the Arkansas regulations as a guide, that would make their operations more productive, and more profitable, over a longer time frame.

Economic geologist Brent Elliott says Texas is in a position that could set the stage for real industry growth and development that even Arkansas lacks. Geoframe CEO Bruce Cutright is urging the Texas legislature to resolve such issues as rights and responsibilities regarding critical minerals and brine. The sticky issue is whether lithium brine is a mere byproduct of oil and gas production or is extracted specifically to recover lithium through direct lithium extraction.

The Ark-La-Tex lithium industry is in its infancy but has potential to revitalize rural and small-town economies – and that dovetails with the goals both of President Trump’s 2018 Rural Prosperity Task Force and 2025’s One Big Beautiful Bill – as well as with his call for rebuilding the domestic critical minerals industry and ending the stifling of mining operations in America.

text:
THE AMERICANS STOP DOING MEMES

That is the condition. That is the stated diplomatic precondition for restarting trade talks between two sovereign nations.

Sir. You have forty one million people in your entire country. There are going to be more memes than that by Thursday. Every man, woman and child in Canada is getting one personally addressed to them, and some of you are getting two.

You did not draw a red line. You placed an order.

Now let me explain your negotiating position, using a car.

You have a car for sale. It is not a beautiful car. It has some rust, the heater works when it feels like it, and you are asking well above book.

There is exactly one buyer in the entire country. One. He lives next door, he has a garage full of cars already, he does not need yours, and both of you know it.

But you have told your girlfriend you are getting a great price. You said it out loud. So now you are standing in the driveway performing toughness for an audience of one who is not the buyer.

He offers. You say no, and add a condition about his behaviour.

He offers less.

You call him a bully in front of the neighbours. He offers less again, and mentions he is thinking of renaming the lake at the end of your street.

And here is the part you already know at two in the morning. You are going to take whatever he offers, because he is the only man on the road with a chequebook, and every day you spend defending your dignity the number goes down.

Doug Ford, meanwhile, has been in the driveway the whole time shouting about turning off the man's electricity, which is worth about a quarter million dollars a day against an economy that produces eighty billion in that same period.

Beauty, eh.

The two of you have become Doug and Bob McKenzie negotiating a trade agreement. Take off, you hoser, we are not selling you the crude. Good day.

Except in Strange Brew the boys accidentally end up owning the brewery, and Canada is not going to accidentally end up owning the refineries, because they are all in Texas and Louisiana and we bought them fair and square.

You have four hundred nineteen billion in goods going south every year. Seventy seven percent of your exports have exactly one destination. Your best province ranks twentieth against American states and Ontario is forty eighth, behind Alabama.

And your opening move was to demand we stop posting.

Mark, my friend, that is not leverage. That is a man in a driveway explaining to the only buyer on earth why he should feel bad about himself.

Take the deal.

And get the elbows down before somebody makes a meme about that too.

🦋

REGIONAL SPORTS ROUNDUP
September 2, 2026

HIGH SCHOOL

TUESDAY NIGHT RECAP
In the Girls Kentucky 2A Championships Section 1 Soccer Tournament, Calloway County advanced with a 2-0 win over Paducah Tilghman. Raylee McClure and Karlyn Provine scored goals with assists from Finley Lencki and Layla Barrow. The Calloway County boys were also successful with a 3-1 win at Madisonville-North Hopkins. 

In volleyball, Caldwell County swept Murray 3-0. 

COLLEGE

TOPPING OFF CEREMONY AT THE BANK
Murray State Athletics marked a major milestone yesterday in the CFSB Center renovation with the placement of the facility’s final steel beam. The topping-off ceremony highlights continued progress on the modernization of the longtime home of Racer basketball and the creation of upgraded experiences and performance spaces for student-athletes, fans and the university community. 

The renovated CFSB Center will introduce premium seating options, including new loge boxes, ledge seating and courtside opportunities. A first-of-its-kind courtside club will offer fans upscale food and beverage options, comfortable seating and views just steps from the court, with a design featuring a rustic Kentucky feel.

SEC GOES TO COURT
The Southeastern Conference is preparing for a courtroom throwdown.  According to CBS Sports, the league is due to face a Louisiana judge on Thursday to fight an order blocking it from punishing schools that sign former pro athletes.  An SEC spokesman says the conference has the right to serve its members as a voluntary association.  The Power Four conferences all passed rules last week barring anyone who participated in an NFL, NBA or WNBA draft, signed a pro contract or appeared on a pro roster from returning to play in college.  The measures were passed after a judge allowed several failed NFL players a fifth year of eligibility.

GREENE CLEARED
Kentucky linebacker Sam Greene is ready to hit the field this weekend.  Yesterday, head coach Will Stein announced Greene will be "fully available" for the game against Youngstown State on Saturday.  The USC transfer came to Kentucky before the start of last season and ended up being out for the rest of the year after suffering an ACL injury in November.  Saturday's home game will kick off at noon CDT. 

PROS

CARDINALS REPORT
Thomas Saggese hit two of the Cardinals' six home runs last night as they beat the Dodgers 13-8 in LA.  Ramon Urias, Jordan Walker, and Joshua Baez also went deep for St. Louis, which snapped a two-game skid.  Michael McGreevy gave up four runs in five frames as he improved to 6-9 with the victory.  Mookie Betts drove in four runs for the Dodgers, who have lost five of seven. 

Game two of the three game series is set for tonight at 9:10 with an 8:15 pregame show airtime on WNBS. The Cardinals will send a to be determined starter against the Dodgers Yoshinobu Yamamoto (12-8, 2.56). 

In other team news, Cardinals announced yesterday that the team has promoted three players, and that catcher Jimmy Crooks was optioned to Memphis following Sunday’s game, as Major League Baseball allows active rosters to expand to 28 players. Joining the Cardinals active roster for last night's series opener in Los Angeles were rookie catcher Leo Bernal, rookie RHP Hancel Rincón, and outfielder Victor Scott. 

TITANS REPORT
The Tennessee Titans made a pair of practice-squad moves Tuesday as they continued shaping the roster for Sunday's season opener against the New York Jets. The Titans signed defensive back Shemar Bartholomew to the practice squad and released defensive back Mario Goodrich from the practice squad. The move leaves Tennessee with its practice squad largely set following Monday's additions. 

The biggest news came last night, when wide receiver Xavier Restrepo returned to the Titans' practice squad after clearing waivers. Restrepo initially made Tennessee's 53-man roster Sunday but was waived Monday to make room for five waiver additions.

PREDS TRADE FORWARD
The Predators are moving on from a forward.  The Devils acquired Luke Evangelista from Nashville yesterday in exchange for a conditional first-round pick in 2028, originally belonging to the Colorado Avalanche.  Nashville is also getting a second rounder from Jersey.

SI RESORT OPENS
The country's first fully branded Sports Illustrated resort is open for business in Nashville.  The 185-suite Music Row property opened this week after a full renovation and rebrand.  The concept is built around sports tourism, putting guests near professional and college games as well as the city's entertainment districts.  A final expansion phase is expected to wrap by November.

text:
A lot of people don't know this but

Before I built my 7 Figure YouTube Agency 

I used to run a meme page for Hasbulla Magomedov that I grew from 0 -> 1.3M Followers while still in High School

And I owe a lot of my success today to this experience 

So here are a few lessons I picked up that I still use today 👇

1. You have to move at the speed of culture

The reason i've been able to generate my clients over $5M in the past 18 months directly off YouTube is because I move at the speed of culture

In the context of the Hasbulla page this meant posting a video of Hasbulla driving recklessly when the entire world was excited for the last Fast and Furious movie 

A caption would be like "My Application to be in Fast Forever" and it would rack in literally 100M views from a single tweet

I apply this same approach to my clients 

Claude Design had just released and within 5 days we had already created a video for my client Max which became one of the highest ranking videos for "Claude Email Design" on YouTube 

If a Content Format is absolutely ripping i'd immediately have a video scripted for my Client Marshall titled  

"I’d Bet my Entire Clothing Brand Marketing Budget on These 4 Videos" 

And this new format would be one of the ones we cover within the overall video

In the meme world it gets you virality

But in business this demonstrates to your ICP that you are extremely tapped into the market and you're the guy/girl they need to be listening to/working with 

Nobody listens to the person who uses examples from 10 years ago

2. Reciprocity means everything

When his team first reached out after I blew the page up to 300K, I was 18 and honestly didn't have much to offer them other than memes

I ran the page for basically free for the first year and a half just to get access to people who were making the money I wanted to make

So what I'd do is just take it upon myself to learn whatever they needed

They needed email marketing, someone to work on their site, designs for a merch drop, I'd go learn that skill and just do it for them for free

the byproduct of that was they started trusting me, and felt so grateful for my work that they started paying me more, giving me referrals, allowing me to use the page as an outreach channel

(The page is what allowed me to sign NBA Hall of Famer Tracy McGrady as my 3rd client ever lol)

Same thing when I picked up my first 10 content clients

Free scripts, free videos, whatever it took to put something real in their hands before I ever asked for a dollar back

I still do this to this day to a degree

Someone asks me for YouTube ideas, or wants to run a concept by me, I'm not charging for that most of the time

I just help, because that's what I'm around all day anyway

And the way I see it, if you do good by people they don't forget it

Either they work with you right away, or they're thinking of you the second they actually need you

3. Effort is a moat

I've believed this since day one

The reason I was able to do a quantum leap and from 0 to 100K followers in my first month on the Hasbulla page is because I turned on post notifications for every single relevant meme page or figure attached to that world

Every time they posted, I was the first one in the replies, whether it was a joke, a funny pic, whatever, just to get as much exposure to my page as possible

It let me borrow traffic from accounts way bigger than mine and use it to amplify what I was already posting

Nowadays you can just set up a bot and ship

But back then you had to actually be on it, manually, for hours

I was on my phone 8-10 hours a day just being a reply guy (an actual term we called people in the meme space)

I still operate the same way with clients today

When I'm writing a script, or reviewing one from my team, I'll spend an extra 30, 45 minutes, an hour, just tightening things, linking better examples, doing whatever it takes to make the videos/and my team better than what our competitors 

It genuinely just takes effort

You can't just outsource that to AI, especially creative work, it's not there yet no matter what anyone tells you

And if you do, trust me we can tell

Because that extra 20 minutes, stacked over a year, over 10 years, it genuinely compounds

There's obviously a lot more I owe to that experience but these were a few things I just felt like sharing

text:
Thank you, Edward. I appreciate your thoughtfulness and agree this has been a very enjoyable debate. Our conversation has forced me to revisit concepts from law school, which has been enjoyable, and I’ve learned things in the course of our discussion, so thank you. I wish this type of cordial debate was more readily available on this hellsite.

I’ll offer some thoughts on your points, but first I wanted to genuinely encourage you to read this piece from the American Enterprise Institute that popped on my feed and made me think of you yesterday. Candidly, it summarizes and addresses many of the issues we’ve analyzed better than I ever could. It’s here: https://t.co/IYahAeP95G

On your first point, I think you’re taking something true—the Constitution preserved substantial state sovereignty—and stretching it too far. Yes, ratification occurred through conventions in the several states, and yes, the Tenth Amendment reserved undelegated powers. But Madison’s own Federalist 39, which you cite, says the new system was federal in its foundation but NATIONAL in the operation of its powers and ultimately “neither a national nor a federal Constitution, but a composition of both.” More importantly, McCullochrejected the proposition that ratification through state conventions meant the federal government was merely the creature of sovereign state governments. Marshall said the Constitution proceeded from the people, was binding on the “State sovereignties,” and created an effective government acting directly upon individuals. That is dual sovereignty, not thirteen independent countries joined by a revocable treaty.

And the constitutional text itself makes the point rather clearly and dramatically. Article I, §10 says states cannot enter treaties, alliances or confederations; coin money; or, without congressional consent, maintain peacetime troops or warships, enter agreements with foreign powers, or wage war except in response to invasion or imminent danger. Article VI then makes valid federal law supreme over contrary state law. Those are some of the most basic attributes of independent national sovereignty expressly denied to the states. So I agree Virginia remained sovereign in important respects. I do not agree it remained sovereign in the same sense as France or Britain, free simply to reclaim every delegated power whenever it chose, or whenever there was ambiguity. A truly sovereign state would be permitted to, for example, freely coin its own currency, but the Constitution specifically forbade that, which objectively points to limiting state sovereignty.

On the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions, again, they prove the compact theory existed. They do not prove unilateral secession was a constitutional remedy. In fact, Madison’s Virginia Resolutions begin by pledging to “maintain and defend” the U.S. Constitution and expressed a “warm attachment” to the Union. When later politicians tried to turn his compact theory into unilateral nullification and secession, Madison rejected them. In 1833 he said secession “at will” violated “a faith solemnly pledged” and that secession justified by intolerable oppression was simply another name for revolution. That distinction matters.

The Declaration of Independence gets you to the same place. Of course people possess an ultimate right to overthrow a government that becomes intolerably oppressive. But that is a revolutionary right outside the existing constitutional order. It is not the same thing as saying the Constitution itself gives every state a legal exit clause. Washington had a right of revolution against Britain, but that did not mean British law contained a provision authorizing colonial independence whenever Virginia thought George III had breached the deal. I also think this line of argument inaccurately conflates the root causes and objectives of the Revolutionary War and the Civil War. Americans prior to the Revolutionary War were subjects of the British Crown and had no representation in their government. They offered Britain opportunities to give them that representation, and if Britain had, it’s likely the war would not have occurred and history would look a lot different. The Civil War, on the other hand, was sparked by South Carolinian aggression, and its main purpose was to preserve slavery. Read the secession articles produced by the states who seceded. They clearly demonstrate that the major thrust was to preserve slavery, not for representation in a functioning democracy or to protect its people. Moreover, this leap you make that “secession extended from colonies to states” is not supported by any text. Again, I think it conflates the motivations for colonial independence with Confederate protection of the institution of slavery. South Carolinians were not subjects of the North being taxed by a monarchy an ocean away without representation in that government.

On Article VII and the Treaty of Paris, the chronology is important, and I don’t think you adequately address it. The Treaty of Paris was signed in 1783 under the Articles of Confederation, and the Articles expressly said each state retained its “sovereignty, freedom and independence.” The Framers then met in 1787 precisely because that loose confederation was failing. The Constitution conspicuously does not repeat that language. Instead it creates a government acting directly on citizens, makes federal law supreme, and strips states of powers like independent diplomacy, currency and war-making. McCulloch later described the transformation explicitly: the Confederation had been an “alliance”; the Constitution replaced it with an effective government possessing “great and sovereign powers.” You cannot simply take Virginia’s status in 1783 and assume nothing constitutionally significant happened four years later. The 1787 Convention met precisely because the Articles of Confederation were unworkable, mostly because the states retained too much power and were unwieldy to manage. Take Revolutionary War debt for example. The federal government could not get certain states to pay, in large part because the federal government was too weak to enforce its mandates. The Convention of 1787 met precisely to make the federal government more powerful and supreme to individual state sovereignty.

Calhoun certainly proves that a sophisticated constitutional theory of unilateral state withdrawal existed. I concede that without hesitation. But Calhoun proves the existence of an argument, not that the argument was correct. Marshall, Madison, Webster and others were making the opposite argument long before the Civil War. Again, you seem to point to this ambiguity as if it provides a permission slip, when the opposite conclusion could just as easily have been reached. But what’s more is that we did reach a conclusion, and the Supreme Court has consistently rejected the notions you put forth. I understand those decisions post-dated the Civil War, but the questions were eventually answered. We know the answers to the test even if they were unclear.

On the replacement of the Articles themselves, I actually think that precedent cuts against treating secession as an ordinary constitutional right. The Articles called their Union “perpetual” and required unanimous consent for alteration. The Framers admittedly departed from those rules. But look at Madison’s defense in Federalist 43: he justified it by “absolute necessity,” self-preservation and the higher law of nature. In other words, an extraordinary constituent/revolutionary act was justified because the old system had failed. He did not say, “Every state has always retained an ordinary constitutional right to withdraw whenever it chooses.” The system that failed that sparked the Civil War was admission of new states to the Union as slave states or free states - a much different issue from the ones that prompted the Convention of 1787.

On your next point, I actually think you identify the weakness in the secession position yourself: the Constitution created a government that operated directly on individuals. That was the enormous break from the Articles. And while Texas v. White definitively resolved unilateral secession after the war, federal supremacy within the federal government’s constitutional sphere was emphatically not invented in 1869. McCullochsaid in 1819 that the Constitution “bound the State sovereignties.” In 1859, again before the war, Ableman v. Boothheld that state sovereignty was “limited and restricted by the Constitution” and described the state and federal governments as distinct sovereignties operating independently within their respective spheres. That is almost a textbook description of the dual-sovereignty position I’ve been arguing.

So I would phrase what Appomattox settled much more narrowly than you do. It settled by force whether the Confederacy would succeed in establishing independence. Texas v. White later settled the particular constitutional question of unilateral secession. Neither event suddenly established that the federal government possessed supreme authority within its delegated sphere. That principle had been in the Constitution from the beginning and repeatedly recognized by SCOTUS decades before the war.

Now, on Lee and Jackson and treason, I think your latest formulation is much stronger because you acknowledge the actual issue: they plainly fought against the United States. Where I still disagree is that their subjective understanding of allegiance can determine whether their allegiance legally existed. If Virginia validly seceded, your argument becomes considerably stronger because Virginians arguably ceased owing allegiance to the United States. If Virginia’s purported secession was legally ineffective, however, their allegiance did not vanish simply because they sincerely believed—or preferred to believe—that Virginia had terminated it. Article III then becomes rather difficult to avoid: they deliberately commanded armies “levying War” against the United States.

And Lee specifically presents a problem for the “good-faith belief that secession was constitutionally legitimate” defense because Lee told us what he believed. Before Virginia seceded he said he did not believe in secession as a constitutional right. He nevertheless decided that if Virginia left, he would follow Virginia. I can appreciate the profound personal conflict that created without converting his personal hierarchy of loyalties into constitutional law.

It’s also plainly accurate that neither Lee nor Jackson was convicted of treason. Jackson died during the war and Lee was indicted but never tried. But absence of a conviction does not establish that the underlying conduct was constitutionally non-treasonous. It establishes that no court entered a criminal judgment against them. Those are different propositions.

On your follow-up point that primary state allegiance was a good-faith belief held by “most people” before the war, I think “most people” is doing too much work. It was unquestionably a powerful belief for many Americans, particularly in the South. But Lee’s own peer group is telling. The NPS identifies nine or more U.S. Army colonels from Virginia in 1861. Lee was the ONLY one who ultimately chose Confederate service. Winfield Scott stayed with the United States. George Thomas stayed. Philip St. George Cooke stayed and summarized his decision: “I owe Virginia little, my country much.” Significant portions of Virginia itself remained Unionist and ultimately fielded thousands of Virginians in more than forty Union regiments. So loyalty to state was real, but it was hardly some universally understood rule that dictated what a Virginian officer was supposed to do. This was something I learned during the course of our debate. Lee was the only US Army Colonel to resign his commission and serve the Confederacy. I think that speaks volumes and significantly undercuts the notion that there was a universal and well-understood ideal that placed the state above the Union.

And the military structure reinforces all this. Lee did not hold a Virginia commission while serving in the Regular Army. He held a United States commission. The prewar Army officer oath required “true allegiance to the United States of America” and obedience to the President of the United States. Virginia indeed had its own militia, but Lee was not serving in it. Lee resigned his U.S. commission before entering Confederate service precisely because those were competing allegiances. The institutional structure itself therefore cuts pretty strongly against the idea that federal military service was somehow derivative of an officer’s primary service to his state.

As for your list of sources, I don’t quarrel with it. I just think several of them demonstrate the existence of the constitutional debate rather than resolve it in favor of secession. Federalist 39 affirmatively describes a mixed federal-national system. Federalist 43 justifies superseding the Articles by necessity and self-preservation. Madison later rejected secession at will. And the Treaty of Paris describes states operating under a governmental structure that the Constitution subsequently and deliberately replaced.

Finally, on the monuments, I certainly would not disparage your relative or your friend. Their reactions are legitimate personal perspectives, just as I think your view is. I can respect their perspectives without agreeing with them. I’d also distinguish memorials to ordinary Confederate dead in cemeteries or battlefields from heroic public monuments to Lee, Jackson or Davis. I don’t view those as quite the question.

Where I still fundamentally disagree is the idea that a government putting someone on a pedestal in shared civic space is simply preserving artistic history and leaving the viewer to decide what it means. Public monuments are selective by their nature. We decide whom to elevate, how to depict them and what to inscribe beneath them. Moving a historically significant statue to a museum is not censorship; arguably it allows more history to be taught because you can explain who erected it, when, why, what the inscriptions mean and what historical movement surrounded its construction. And moreover, arguing that statues should remain so we don’t “erase our history” assumes that the public squares these statues inhabit tell the WHOLE history, such that one could view the statue on context. Often, these Confederate monuments offer no such context to the Union ideals or the issue of slavery, so objective learning from the monuments alone is difficult if not impossible. Last, you use the term “art” here pretty loosely. Monuments are a type of art, sure, but they serve a separate societal purpose, which is elevate and glorify the people depicted by the statues themselves. It’s not a sculpture in a garden allowing for fresh and subjective consideration.

And I still come back to your own proposed monument to those fourteen Black Revolutionary War Patriots, because I think your original description was exactly right. You said you wanted it “to honor them, their service, and to provide inspiration for the next generation.” Precisely. That’s what monuments do.

Thanks again for the discussion. This was both enjoyable and insightful.

text:
< Be John Marshall
< Born 1755, Virginia frontier
< No formal schooling until you're nearly grown
< Six weeks of law lectures at William & Mary. That's your legal education.
< You fight in the Revolution. Valley Forge. Brandywine. You survive.
< Return to Virginia, pass the bar, start practicing
< 1788: you argue for ratifying the Constitution. Virginia listens.
< Washington offers you Attorney General. You decline.
< Adams offers you Secretary of War. You decline.
< Adams offers you Secretary of State. Fine.
< January 1801: Adams offers you Chief Justice. You accept.
< You are still Secretary of State. You do both jobs simultaneously.
< Jefferson wins the presidency. You swear him in. He despises you.
< Marbury v. Madison, 1803. You rule against your own party's petitioner.
< Then you write that the Court can void unconstitutional laws. Nowhere in the Constitution does it say this.
< Jefferson is furious. Congress tries to impeach your colleague Chase as a warning shot.
< Chase is acquitted. You serve 34 more years.
< You write over 500 opinions. You lose almost no fights that matter.
< You die in 1829. The Liberty Bell cracks ringing for your funeral.

Six weeks of law school. You invented judicial review out of whole cloth and dared anyone to stop you.

No one did.

The Constitution means what John Marshall said it means, and we are all still living inside that fact.

text:
Denmark’s Monstrous Human Rights Abuses in Greenland

Copenhagen took Greenlanders’ children, violated their bodies, and forfeited any right to rule their distant colony. Greenlanders want independence, but can’t afford it. There’s a solution.

Amarok Petersen was 13 years old when Danish doctors implanted an IUD in her body. No one told her. She discovered it only when she was 27, after years of severe uterine problems, when another doctor finally found the device. By then, the choice to have children had been stolen from her. Years later, she learned that doctors had also removed her fallopian tubes without telling her.

“The Danes don’t see us as humans,” she said.

Last week, two expert investigations put the weight of an official record behind what Petersen and thousands of other Greenlandic women — out of a total population of just 57,000 — had tried to tell for years. Denmark’s treatment of Greenlanders was not “benevolent stewardship” marred by “a handful of mistakes.” It was colonial abuse inflicted on their bodies, their children, their families and their sovereignty.

It also conveniently produced exactly the result Copenhagen wanted: Greenlanders’ birthrate collapsed, the growth of the native population slowed sharply, the percentage of the population that’s Danish thus increased, and Denmark’s annual costs to maintain the colony were controlled.

The new data demolishes Copenhagen’s claim to be Greenland’s benevolent guardian. Denmark has forfeited the moral authority — and the moral right — to rule the island. Greenland’s future rightfully belongs to the Greenlanders. The problem is, they can’t afford the independence most of them want.

There’s a solution.

Their Bodies, But Not Their Choice

Denmark’s forced contraception campaign was staggering in scale. By the end of 1970 alone, nearly half of all women of childbearing age or younger had been fitted with IUDs, mostly without their knowledge or consent. 

In addition to IUDs, the program included contraceptive injections and other interventions, largely disguised as other procedures. This crime against humanity continued through 1991, when Greenland finally wrested its health system from its colonial overlord’s control.

The new human-rights investigation heard from 354 women describing 488 separate incidents. Of 410 reported IUD insertions, 300 women said they had never consented. In another 63 cases, investigators had no consent information at all. 

Nearly one-third of the women were 14 or younger at the time; more than half were minors. Some were just 12 years old.

These were not adults making informed medical decisions. They were schoolgirls summoned to clinics, fitted with devices they did not understand, and sent home in pain. Some bled. Some developed infections. Some suffered lasting physical and psychological damage. Some, like Petersen, lost the ability to bear children even after discovering what had been done.

One team of investigators found reasonable grounds to believe that Denmark’s conduct in imposing measures to prevent births met the definition contained in the Genocide Convention. The investigators stopped short of finding genocide because they could not establish specific intent for that exact crime. That distinction will matter in court, reducing possible claims against the Danish government. It does not rescue Denmark’s reputation.

Nor does Copenhagen seriously dispute the charge. In September 2025, Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen acknowledged that thousands of women and girls had received IUDs, many against their will. She admitted that Greenlanders had been subjected to systematic discrimination precisely because they were Greenlandic. 

To her credit, she apologized on behalf of Denmark. But it’s far too little, far too late.

Denmark treated Greenlandic women not as patients or citizens, but as a herd to be culled. Petersen put it more plainly: “They took our resources. They took our bodies. And then they told us to thank them.”

Then Denmark Took The Children They Had

A state that believed it could decide which, if any, Greenlandic women would be allowed to become mothers also presumed to decide which Greenlandic mothers were allowed to keep their children.

The United Nations has reported that Inuit children from Greenland living in Denmark were seven times more likely than Danish-born children to be taken and placed outside the home. Danish authorities relied on standardized psychological and “parenting competency” tests developed for Danish parents, in the Danish language and within Danish cultural assumptions. 

They then used those tests to judge Greenlanders whose language, emotional expression, extended-family structure and child-rearing traditions were profoundly different.

The result was both predictable and monstrous. Danish institutions defined Danish behavior as normal, interpreted Greenlandic standards as inferior, and took Greenlandic children from their families on that basis. 

Mothers described being assessed without adequate interpreters. One says she was forbidden to speak Greenlandic to her twin sons during visits. The boys eventually lost their mother tongue as well as their mother.

It was a systematic effort to erase the Greenlandic population and culture for the benefit of an imperial master.

Denmark only abandoned the standardized tests for Greenlandic families in 2025, replacing them with assessments by a specialized unit with Greenlandic language and cultural competence. 

Yet mere months later, authorities removed Ivana Nikoline Brønlund’s newborn daughter approximately one hour after birth without applying the new procedure. Denmark’s Social Minister called the failure a serious error. Yet only after widespread political outrage was the decision reversed, allowing mother and child to reunite.

This is not ancient history: this is yesterday.

Greenland Wants Independence. But It Can’t Afford It.

Greenlanders have been voting their way toward independence for nearly half a century. Understandably, more than 70 percent approved Home Rule in 1979. In 2008, 75.5 percent approved Self-Government — an arrangement that formally recognized Greenlanders as a people with the right to self-determination, and that established a legal path to full sovereignty. 

By January 2025, a Verian poll found that 84 percent wanted independence, and 56 percent would vote for it even if the referendum were held immediately.

The hesitation is not the destination: it’s the price. Independence is expensive, and as badly as Denmark underfunds its colony, its colony doesn’t have the money to replace what it does spend. Independence means more than raising a flag. 

A sovereign country must finance its government, build infrastructure, create and maintain embassies around the world, provide social services and defend an enormous, resource-rich island sitting astride the Arctic and Atlantic approaches to North America. 

Greenland cannot do all of that alone. Denmark adds very little, but it’s far more than Greenland can do for itself.

So Greenland is not debating whether it should be free. It’s debating how to survive afterward.

The answer, of course, is a Compact of Free Association with the United States. It’s a model the U.S. has used successfully for and with Pacific nations such as Palau, Micronesia and the Marshall Islands. Each is a sovereign, independent nation. But each also receives many of the benefits of being part of the United States, defense included.

Citizens of these three COFA nations may live and work indefinitely in the United States, as nonimmigrants without a visa. They can qualify for American benefits ranging from Pell Grants and work-study programs to Medicare and Social Security. They may join the U.S. military. If disaster strikes, FEMA shows up. America invests and creates jobs in their countries. 

A COFA provides all the benefits of inclusion in the world’s most powerful economy but without giving up independence. It also provides all the benefits of independence without the costs.

It’s genuinely “have your cake and eat it too.”

For Greenlanders, a COFA means independence without strategic helplessness. American capital and technology, far greater than anything Denmark can provide, would flow in to build the ports, airports, power systems, telecommunications, housing and processing facilities, all employing Greenland’s citizens and providing futures for its children.

Greenland’s vast deposits of rare earth elements, hydrocarbons and other minerals could create high-paying jobs and a booming local economy rather than leave the island dependent on a stingy annual subsidy. Its fisheries could be processed at home rather than shipped away so others capture the value. Its tourism — currently a fraction of Alaska’s — could make the country a fortune: just ask Iceland.

Greenland could even become the Arctic answer to Bermuda or the Caymans: a sovereign financial center inside the American economic system, with easy access to both New York and London. The nation could attract offshore wealth beyond anything it has ever imagined. 

Perhaps even more important, Greenland's young people would no longer have to choose between dependence and emigration. Greenlanders could build a rich, modern country all their own.

So What Would America Get Out of This?

For America, the advantages are every bit as substantial. A free and friendly Greenland would secure the northern approaches to the United States, anchor the Greenland-Iceland-UK Gap, protect emerging Arctic sea lanes and enhance early warning, missile defense, space surveillance and North Atlantic monitoring.

A COFA would give American companies access to critical minerals outside China’s control while denying Beijing or Moscow the chance to turn Greenlandic poverty into a strategic foothold threatening the approaches to North America.

America does not need to actually own Greenland. It needs Greenland to be free, prosperous and able to choose a durable partnership with America. That is partnership, not colonialism: indeed, it would replace the current colonialism with a true partnership. Greenlanders would own Greenland, while both nations become richer and safer.

This solves Greenlanders’ long-term problem even more than America’s. But it also solves a problem that almost no one in today’s ahistorical political class grasps. Despite its shameful behavior, Denmark is America’s friend today. But no one can guarantee the future.

The peaceful North Atlantic order is a constructed alignment, not a law of nature. The structure of power and interests may change. The map does not. And leaders should not base the security of those entrusted to them on utopian dreams or “permanent” alliances and institutions.

The example of Diego Garcia is a stark reminder. America chose Diego Garcia, its most vital Indian Ocean base, in part because of Britain’s “unquestioned sovereignty” over the island. Britain remains one of America’s closest allies. 

Yet Britain's socialist government has signed a treaty to transfer sovereignty over the Chagos Archipelago to Chinese-aligned Mauritius. It assures the United States and its own people that all may rely on “ironclad” treaty protections for continued American and British access to the base. Yet that’s obviously nonsense.

Britain did not have to become America’s enemy to alter the strategic arrangement on which our security relies. Governments change. Treaties change. Interests change. Alliances change. Geography does not.

Greenland will remain astride North America’s Arctic and Atlantic approaches no matter who governs in Copenhagen or Nuuk five, 50, or 100 years from now. Nations do not have the luxury of assuming every future government will play nice forever. American statesmen must plan for the geography their grandchildren will inherit, not merely for the diplomatic comfort of the present.

Denmark’s abuses answer the moral question. Greenlandic independence answers the colonial question. Free association with America answers the economic and strategic questions. It also enables what last week’s reports make clearly necessary, but which would be impossible without American help.

Denmark’s rule must end. Greenlanders must be free. But for that to happen, America alone can offer them a future in which independence means sovereignty, prosperity and security — not poverty, vulnerability or a new Chinese master.

Crypto made new friends in U.S. primaries, but focus now shifts to general election

The crypto industry’s political playbook is working. With Massachusetts Congressman Jake Auchincloss surviving his primary challenge, the industry-backed political action committee Fairshake has now backed a clean sweep of winning candidates in this cycle’s U.S. primaries. But the real test—and the real money—now shifts to the general election in November, where control of Congress hangs in the balance and digital asset policy is finally a ballot-box issue.

What Happened

Fairshake, the super PAC funded by major crypto players like Coinbase, a16z, and Ripple, added Auchincloss to its win column after the Massachusetts Democrat fended off a progressive challenger. Auchincloss, who has positioned himself as a pro-crypto voice within his party, now advances to the general election in a safely Democratic district—essentially guaranteeing his return to Washington.

The primary results cap a strategic phase for Fairshake, which has poured tens of millions into races on both sides of the aisle. The committee’s approach has been notably bipartisan, supporting candidates who demonstrate a constructive stance on digital asset legislation regardless of party affiliation. That strategy has paid off so far, with every Fairshake-backed candidate winning their primary contest.

Now the PAC is redirecting its war chest toward November’s general election battles, where the Federal Election Commission records show the industry has already committed significant resources to competitive districts in New York, California, and Ohio.

Why This Matters for Crypto

The primary wins are a signal, not the finish line. For the crypto market, the significance lies in what these victories represent: a maturing political operation that can deliver results. When an industry demonstrates it can influence election outcomes, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle tend to become more receptive to its policy priorities.

The immediate market impact is subtle but real. Regulatory clarity—or the lack of it—remains one of the largest overhangs on digital asset valuations. Every primary win for a pro-crypto candidate incrementally improves the odds that the next Congress will pass meaningful market structure legislation. That expectation alone can influence institutional sentiment, even if it doesn't move spot prices overnight.

For the broader crypto ecosystem, the stakes in November could not be higher. A Congress with a working majority favorable to digital assets could finally deliver the regulatory framework that exchanges, custodians, and institutional investors have been demanding for years. Conversely, a hostile Congress could embolden regulators to pursue aggressive enforcement actions, chilling innovation and pushing projects offshore.

What Traders Should Watch

While primary results rarely move markets directly, the general election campaign season will produce signals that traders should monitor closely. Polling data in key swing districts with competitive House races will offer the clearest window into whether the crypto industry's political investments are paying off.

Watch for legislative markers as well. If the CFTC or the SEC signals progress on joint rulemaking in the coming weeks, that could indicate bipartisan momentum carrying into the lame-duck session. Any committee hearings scheduled before the election will be scrutinized for tone and substance—lawmakers running for re-election often adjust their rhetoric based on their district's crypto demographics.

On-chain metrics and derivatives positioning will tell their own story. Look for institutional flows into regulated futures products as a proxy for confidence in the post-election regulatory environment. A sustained increase in open interest on CME bitcoin futures, for example, often precedes institutional deployment of capital once political uncertainty resolves.

Market Sentiment Analysis

The current sentiment reading is NEUTRAL, and that assessment holds up under scrutiny. On one hand, the primary wins provide a tangible positive for the regulatory outlook. On the other, markets are notoriously forward-looking, and the general election remains genuinely competitive with outcomes far from certain.

Short-term, expect continued range-bound trading as the market digests political headlines alongside macroeconomic data. The long-term outlook, however, carries an asymmetric skew: if the crypto-friendly candidates win in November, the regulatory clarity that follows could unlock a wave of institutional adoption. If they lose, the industry faces another two years of legal uncertainty and enforcement-driven volatility.

For now, the smart play is patience. The market has priced in neither a decisive victory nor a defeat for the crypto agenda. That leaves room for significant repricing once actual election results arrive.

Frequently Asked Questions

How does Fairshake's primary success translate to general election influence?
Fairshake has demonstrated it can deploy capital effectively in primary contests, which builds credibility with donors and political operatives. That track record makes it easier to raise additional funds for general election races, where the stakes are higher and the costs are greater. The PAC's bipartisan approach also gives it leverage regardless of which party controls Congress after November.

What specific crypto legislation is at stake in the November election?
The most significant pending items include market structure legislation that would clarify whether digital assets are securities or commodities, stablecoin regulation, and potential amendments to how the SEC oversees crypto exchanges. A favorable Congress could also push for clearer guidelines on custody, taxation, and cross-border transactions—all of which remain murky under current law.

Should retail traders change their strategy based on primary results?
Generally, no. Primary outcomes are just one input among many affecting crypto prices, and they rarely trigger immediate market moves. Traders should focus on their existing strategies while monitoring the general election as a scheduled catalyst event. Position sizing around known dates like Election Day is prudent, but reacting to every political headline is a recipe for overtrading and unnecessary losses.

text:
I am not a lawyer, but this is my understanding of the "Tuey-Rodriguez" charge. Corrections and clarifications welcome.
It's a jury instruction.
When a jury can't agree, they tell the judge they're stuck. The judge can read them the Tuey-Rodriguez charge. Massachusetts named it after two cases, one from 1851 and one from 1973. Other states call it the "dynamite charge," because it's meant to blow open a deadlock.
The instruction says, in simple terms: a juror's vote has to be their own honest belief, not just going along with the group. But the jurors should return to the room, listen to each other in good faith, and reach agreement if they honestly can.
The instruction is usually given once. Repeating it, or adding to it, can start to look like the judge pressuring the jury. That can get a conviction overturned later.
Sending the jury back to keep working is a separate rule. After the first report of deadlock, the judge can send them back. After the second, the judge cannot send them back again unless the jurors themselves agree to continue. The one exception is a question about the law, which does not count against them.
If they still can't agree, the result is a mistrial. That is not an acquittal. It means this jury could not reach a verdict, and prosecutors then decide whether to retry the case with a new jury, offer a plea, or drop the charges.

text:
Pittsburgh 2026 Rapid Preview

OFFENSE:
Eli Holstein came in last yr as QB1 but benched after 4 games due to turnover woes. True Fr Mason Heintschel took over and led them to 6-2 finish, causing Holstein to transfer. Heintschel can make plays w/ legs as well but needs to improve on 20 TWP to just 13 BTT.

RB Desmond Reid battled injuries all yr, but another true Fr Ja'Kyrian Turner stepped up as well to lead in rushing (had 200 in upset over GT). Turner is back and should only improve as the top dog from Week 1, but is only returner with 10+ carries. 5th yr WKU transfer La'Vell Wright figures to back up but not a ton of depth.

Top 2 WR depart but #3 Cataurus Hicks is back after a solid yr as a full-time starter. Censere Lee was part of group that came from WCU with OC Kade Bell in '24 and played a role that year, but hardly played in '25 due to injury. He's healthy and they add a new WCU transfer in Malik Knight. Bryce Yates is one to watch as well (18.4 ypc last year).

Carson Kent (Oklahoma) and Elijah Lagg (UAB) will replace starting TE Justin Holmes. Each bring more blocking but receiving at this position drops. 

The O-Line had 3 guys play the entire the yr, but had to shuffle the other two positions due to injury and struggled at times. 2 of those 3 are back (BJ Williams and Ryan Baer) and this unit as a whole is very experienced. Should be improved if they have better health.

DEFENSE:
This D-Line was stout against the run last yr, ranking 3rd nationally in ypc allowed. Will be really good again with 3 starters back plus Nick James who was basically co-starter. Should be able to go two-deep across the line as well.

Big story of this D is the loss of two star LBs Biles (Texas) and Louis (NFL). Impossible to replace but bring in starters from Purdue and Memphis to try to soften the blow. 

They do return their 3rd LB and tackler Braylan Lovelace who has seen increased role each yr, and actually led D in snaps last season by a wide margin. Cameron Lindsey started 3 games and performed well. While this unit doesn't have same star power, may be more playable depth.

Secondary loses 3 starters but the two highest graded PFF defenders return, S Cruce Brookins and CB Shawn Lee. Both are exciting players but need others to step up back here. There are a couple other returners who will battle for time, along with Auburn transfer Raion Strader who was 1st Tm All-MAC before.

SCHEDULE:
They don't leave Heinz Field (proper name) until October. The first two are noncon games that aren't layups; Miami OH has made 3 straight MAC title games and UCF should be better in Year 2 under Frost.

Starting 4-0 AND protecting home field in ACC is crucial because the road schedule is tough... Miami, L'Ville, VT on a Friday night and cross country at Cal to close the season.

OVERALL OUTLOOK:
Everybody seems to love Heintschel, but if you look at numbers between he and Holstein last year they're very comparable. I understand though the former was a true Fr so offers more upside, while latter was a 3rd yr college guy so maybe reached his ceiling. We will see.

I love the experience and depth on both LOS and the RB Turner, but there are certainly questions elsewhere. You’re replacing a ton of production across the back 7, can guys step up? And I'm not sold on the WRs just yet. But if one or both get answered, the early schedule sets up to create some momentum heading into the heart of ACC play.
